title: Two Wheels and a Revolution: The Early History of the Bicycle
titleCn: 两个轮子的革命：自行车早期史

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few machines are as familiar as the bicycle, yet its basic form took most of the nineteenth century to settle. The story usually begins in 1817, when Karl von Drais, a German forestry official, demonstrated what he called a 'running machine'. It had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a simple steering bar, but no pedals: the rider sat astride it and pushed against the ground with his feet. Some historians have suggested that Drais was looking for a substitute for the horse after a series of poor harvests had made animal feed scarce and expensive, although the evidence for this link is indirect. In Britain, where the device was known as the 'hobby-horse', young men of means paid to ride it in special halls, but the craze faded within a few years, partly because riders were accused of endangering pedestrians on the pavements.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Pedals did not appear until the 1860s, when a workshop in Paris began attaching cranks directly to the front wheel of a two-wheeled machine. Who first had the idea remains disputed, but the resulting 'velocipede' sold in large numbers in France and was soon copied abroad. It was not a comfortable vehicle. Its frame was made of heavy iron, its wooden wheels were surrounded by iron bands, and on the cobbled streets of the period every stone was transmitted directly to the rider. English speakers gave it the nickname 'boneshaker', and the name was well deserved. Nevertheless, the velocipede proved that a person could balance on two wheels while propelling them with the feet, which many people had doubted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Because the pedals were fixed to the front wheel, one turn of the pedals produced one turn of the wheel. The only way to go faster was therefore to make that wheel bigger, and during the 1870s manufacturers did exactly that. On the machines that came to be known as 'ordinaries', and much later as 'penny-farthings' after two British coins of very different sizes, the front wheel could be as much as one and a half metres across, while the rear wheel was tiny. Lighter steel frames and solid rubber tyres made these bicycles faster and smoother than the boneshaker, but they were also dangerous. A rider sat high above the front wheel, and if it struck a stone or a hole, he could be thrown head first over the handlebars, an accident so common that it had its own name: 'taking a header'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The solution came from Coventry, in the English Midlands, where in 1885 John Kemp Starley produced a machine he called the Rover. Its two wheels were of roughly equal size, the rider sat between them, and the pedals turned the rear wheel by means of a chain. By choosing gears of different sizes, the designer could make the rear wheel turn several times for every turn of the pedals, so a large wheel was no longer needed for speed. Because the rider's feet could now reach the ground, these machines were sold as 'safety bicycles'. The last major problem was comfort, and this was addressed in 1888, when John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet working in Belfast, developed an air-filled tyre for his son's tricycle.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What followed in the 1890s was a boom of remarkable scale. Mass production in Britain, France and the United States brought prices down, and for the first time millions of people who could not afford to keep a horse had a means of private transport. The effects on women were particularly striking. Long, heavy skirts were impractical on a bicycle, and many female cyclists adopted shorter skirts or loose trousers, provoking fierce debate in the press. More importantly, the bicycle allowed women to travel without a chaperone, and campaigners for women's rights frequently described it as a tool of independence. Some doctors warned that cycling would damage women's health, but such warnings did little to slow its popularity.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Cyclists also changed the roads themselves. By the late nineteenth century, many country roads in Britain and North America were in a poor state, because the railways had taken over most long-distance traffic and there was little reason to maintain them. Organised cyclists began to campaign for better surfaces. In the United States, a national cycling association led what became known as the Good Roads Movement, publishing maps, lobbying politicians and arguing that smooth roads would benefit farmers as well as riders. Ironically, when motor cars appeared a few years later, they inherited the improved roads that cyclists had fought for, and soon pushed bicycles to the edges of them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The bicycle's influence extended beyond transport. Building lightweight, precise machines in large numbers required new techniques, including steel tubing, ball bearings and the accurate cutting of gears, and many of the engineers and firms that mastered them later moved into the manufacture of cars. The most famous example is that of the Wright brothers, who ran a bicycle shop in Ohio and used the money and skills it provided to build their first aircraft. In much of Europe and North America, the bicycle was later overshadowed by the car, but in recent decades cities from Copenhagen to Paris have invested heavily in cycle lanes. Two centuries after Drais pushed himself along with his feet, his invention is once again being treated as a serious answer to urban problems.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, sleep was regarded as a period of inactivity, a nightly switching-off of the brain that needed little explanation. Physicians and philosophers wrote at length about dreams, but the state of sleep itself attracted far less attention. This began to change in the twentieth century, when it became possible to record the electrical activity of the brain through sensors placed on the scalp. The recordings showed that the sleeping brain is far from idle. Its activity rises and falls in regular patterns throughout the night, and some of those patterns are as intense as anything seen during waking hours. Sleep, it turned out, was not a single state but a sequence of quite different ones.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most important discovery came in the early 1950s from a laboratory in Chicago. Researchers observing sleeping volunteers noticed that, at intervals during the night, their eyes began to move rapidly from side to side beneath closed lids. When the volunteers were woken during these periods, they usually reported vivid dreams; when woken at other times, they rarely did. This phase became known as rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. Curiously, although the brain is highly active during REM sleep, most of the body's muscles are temporarily paralysed, which may prevent sleepers from acting out their dreams. The remaining phases, in which the eyes are still, were grouped together as non-REM sleep.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It soon became clear that these phases follow a predictable order. A sleeper passes from light non-REM sleep into deeper stages, in which breathing slows and the person becomes difficult to wake, before returning to lighter sleep and then entering a period of REM. One complete cycle takes roughly ninety minutes, and a typical night contains four to six of them. The cycles are not identical, however. Deep non-REM sleep dominates the first half of the night, while REM periods become longer towards morning. This explains why people who are woken early often feel that they were interrupted in the middle of a dream, and why a short night tends to reduce REM sleep more than deep sleep.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The timing of sleep is controlled by an internal clock, a small group of cells deep in the brain that keeps a rhythm of roughly twenty-four hours even in the absence of external cues. Left entirely alone, this clock tends to drift slightly, so it is reset every day mainly by light entering the eyes. In the evening, as light fades, the body releases a hormone called melatonin, which signals that it is time to sleep. Artificial light can delay this signal, and many sleep researchers advise reducing the use of bright screens in the hour before bed, although the size of the effect in everyday life is still debated.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The internal clock does not stay the same throughout life. During adolescence, it shifts later by an hour or more, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and find it hard to wake early. This change appears to be biological rather than simply a matter of habit, since it has been observed in many different cultures. It creates an obvious conflict with school timetables that begin early in the morning. Several education authorities that have moved the start of the school day later have reported that students sleep longer and are more alert in class, and some have also recorded better attendance, although results have varied from place to place.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why we sleep at all remains one of the central questions of biology. One well-supported idea is that sleep helps to consolidate memories. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity from the day, strengthening some connections and weakening others, so that useful information is kept while trivial details are discarded. A more recent proposal is that sleep allows the brain to clear away waste products that build up during waking hours; experiments on mice found that fluid flows through brain tissue much more freely during sleep. Most researchers now believe that sleep has several functions rather than one, which may help to explain why some form of sleep has been observed in almost every animal that scientists have examined.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whatever its purposes, the consequences of losing sleep are well documented. After a single night without sleep, attention and reaction times decline to a level comparable to that of a person who has drunk alcohol, and people are often poor judges of how impaired they are. Over longer periods, short sleep has been linked to a higher risk of several illnesses, though cause and effect can be hard to separate. It is sometimes assumed that people in the past slept better than we do. One historian has argued that, before artificial lighting became common, many Europeans slept in two separate periods, waking for an hour or so in the middle of the night. If he is right, the single unbroken night that we regard as normal may itself be a relatively modern habit.

title: Minds in the Sea: The Puzzling Intelligence of the Octopus
titleCn: 海中的心智：章鱼令人费解的智慧

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Among animals without backbones, the octopus stands out. It belongs to the molluscs, the same group as snails, clams and oysters, yet it behaves in ways that seem to have more in common with mammals and birds. There are around 300 known species, ranging from creatures small enough to sit on a fingernail to the giant Pacific octopus, whose arms can span several metres. Over millions of years, the ancestors of octopuses lost the protective shell that most molluscs still carry. Many biologists believe this loss was a turning point: an animal with a soft, unprotected body had to find food and avoid predators by being flexible, inventive and difficult to catch.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That flexibility is supported by an unusually large nervous system. A common octopus has around 500 million nerve cells, a number comparable to that of a dog, but the way these cells are arranged is quite unlike anything found in animals with backbones. Only around a third of them are in the central brain; the rest are distributed through the eight arms. Each arm can taste and feel the objects it touches and appears able to carry out some actions with little direction from the centre. Researchers have even observed arms that had been separated from the body continuing to respond to touch and to grasp pieces of food, which suggests that a great deal of decision-making happens locally.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The best known of the octopus's abilities is its skill at disguise. Its skin contains thousands of cells filled with coloured pigment, each of which can be expanded or squeezed by tiny muscles, allowing the animal to change its appearance in a fraction of a second. It can also raise small bumps on its skin to imitate the texture of rock or seaweed. Remarkably, laboratory tests suggest that most octopuses cannot distinguish colours, because their eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive cell. How they manage to match their surroundings so precisely remains unclear. One possibility under investigation is that the skin itself can detect light, since proteins used for vision in the eye have also been found there.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Octopuses are also skilled problem-solvers. In laboratories they have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach the crabs inside, and in aquariums they have a reputation as escape artists, squeezing through gaps barely wider than their eyes. Some keepers report that individual octopuses respond differently to different people, squirting water at one member of staff while ignoring others. In the wild, divers off the coast of Indonesia filmed octopuses carrying halves of coconut shells across the seabed and later assembling them into a shelter. Because the animals carried the shells for some distance before using them, many researchers regarded this as a clear case of tool use, a behaviour once thought to be limited to humans and a few other animals.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These abilities are all the more surprising because most octopuses live very short lives, often only one or two years. Females of many species lay a single batch of eggs and then guard them continuously, cleaning them and keeping predators away. During this time, which in some deep-sea species can last for years, the mother typically stops eating, and she dies soon after the young hatch. Males usually die within months of mating. As a result, young octopuses never meet their parents and cannot learn from them, unlike the young of most intelligent mammals and birds. Everything an octopus knows must be either inherited or discovered for itself.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This combination of intelligence and short life presents a puzzle for biologists. In mammals, large brains are usually associated with long lives and complex social groups, in which there is time to learn and others to learn from. The octopus has neither. One explanation links its intelligence to the loss of the shell. A soft-bodied animal hunting in a complex environment such as a reef faces an enormous variety of problems, from opening shells to escaping fish that want to eat it, and the ability to solve them quickly may have been worth the cost of a large nervous system, even if the animal lives for only a year or two.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Growing recognition of octopus intelligence has begun to influence law and policy. In the early 2020s, after an independent review of the scientific evidence, the United Kingdom included octopuses, together with squid, cuttlefish, crabs and lobsters, in legislation that recognises animals as sentient beings, able to experience pain and distress. The decision has been cited in debates elsewhere, particularly over proposals to farm octopuses for food on a commercial scale. Critics of such farms argue that keeping solitary, curious animals in crowded tanks would cause them serious suffering. Supporters reply that farming could reduce pressure on wild populations. The debate is likely to continue as more is learned about what it is like to be an octopus.

They made the shells into a new shape.

evidence.quote: Because the animals carried the shells for some distance before using them, many researchers regarded this as a clear case of tool use

questions.prompt: According to paragraph E, what happens to many female octopuses after they lay eggs?

options.text: They leave the eggs to hatch alone.
They hunt more often to build up strength.
They stop eating while they protect the eggs.
They lay a second batch the following year.

questions.explanation: E 段：雌章鱼产下一批卵后持续守护，这期间通常停止进食（stops eating），幼体孵化后不久死去。对应 C。A 与原文相反；B、D 原文没提，而且原文说只产一批卵。

evidence.quote: the mother typically stops eating, and she dies soon after the young hatch

questions.prompt: Why does the writer describe octopus intelligence as a puzzle?

options.text: Octopuses have smaller brains than most fish.
Octopuses lack the features usually linked with large brains in mammals.
Octopuses live in environments with few problems to solve.
Octopus intelligence seems to decline with age.

questions.explanation: F 段：哺乳动物的大脑袋通常与长寿命和复杂的社会群体相关，而章鱼两者都没有（The octopus has neither）。对应 B。C 与原文相反（原文说环境复杂、问题繁多）；A、D 原文没提。

evidence.quote: In mammals, large brains are usually associated with long lives and complex social groups, in which there is time to learn and others to learn from. The octopus has neither.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph G?

options.text: to describe how octopuses are farmed
to argue that octopus farming should be banned
to compare octopuses with crabs and lobsters
to show how scientific findings have affected law and public debate

questions.explanation: G 段首句点题：对章鱼智力的认识开始影响法律和政策，随后讲英国立法和养殖争议。对应 D。B 不对，作者只并列了反对方和支持方的观点，没有表态；A、C 只是段中细节。

evidence.quote: Growing recognition of octopus intelligence has begun to influence law and policy.

groups.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

summary.title: A short and solitary life
summary.text: Unlike most molluscs, octopuses no longer have a protective {q10}, and many biologists see this as a turning point in their evolution. A common octopus has around 500 million nerve cells, roughly the same number as a {q11}. Most octopuses live for only a year or two. Females of many species produce just one batch of {q12} and die soon after the young hatch, so young octopuses never meet their {q13} and must either inherit what they know or work it out alone.

questions.explanation: A 段：章鱼的祖先失去了大多数软体动物至今仍有的保护性外壳（the protective shell）。填 shell。

evidence.quote: the ancestors of octopuses lost the protective shell that most molluscs still carry

questions.explanation: B 段：普通章鱼约有 5 亿个神经细胞，数量与狗相当（comparable to that of a dog）。填 dog。

evidence.quote: a number comparable to that of a dog

questions.explanation: E 段：许多物种的雌章鱼只产一批卵（a single batch of eggs）。填 eggs，注意用复数。

evidence.quote: Females of many species lay a single batch of eggs

questions.explanation: E 段：幼体从未见过父母，也无法向它们学习（never meet their parents）。填 parents。

evidence.quote: young octopuses never meet their parents and cannot learn from them
